initial_presentation: A ten-month-old Hispanic girl was brought to the pediatric otolaryngology clinic due to an observed asymmetry in her face. The mother reported noticing an uneven movement of the lower lip since birth, which became more evident when the child smiled or cried. The rest of the facial movements were symmetrical. The child was born at full term without any complications, and the mother had no medical issues. Both the child's past medical history and family history were unremarkable. During the physical examination, the child appeared well and showed no signs of respiratory distress. The otologic, nasal, and oral cavity examinations were all normal. The face appeared symmetrical when at rest. However, there was an inward deviation of the right lower lip when the child smiled. The function of the facial nerve, assessed through frowning, forehead wrinkling, eye closure, nasolabial fold depth, and tearing, was symmetrical. The neurodevelopmental examination was normal.

A 33-year-old Caucasian female arrived at the emergency department with persistent non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting and generalized fatigue for three days. She mentioned experiencing similar vomiting episodes lasting 2-3 days every two months, which were alleviated by ondansetron. Additionally, she reported numbness and tingling in her feet for the past year. There was no history of fever, dizziness, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or shortness of breath. She denied smoking or illicit drug use but had a history of heavy alcohol consumption. Her medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and rheumatoid arthritis.
A 41-year-old male reported experiencing decreased vision, haloes, and visual distortion for the past 13 years. His brother had similar visual issues.

A 6-day-old male neonate, born at full term via vaginal delivery, exhibited nonbilious vomiting starting on the 2nd day of life. The infant passed a small amount of meconium but had no subsequent bowel movements. Mild upper abdominal distention was noted after feeding. The neonate was active, alert, and did not have a fever. The mother had multiple previous pregnancies and received adequate antenatal care. The birth weight was 2.

A male patient aged between 55 and 60 years reported experiencing episodes of vertigo and tinnitus over a period of 3 years. The patient was on a daily dose of 4 mg silodosin for benign prostate hyperplasia. Each vertigo episode lasted approximately 30 minutes and was associated with nausea, vomiting, and tinnitus in the right ear. These episodes frequently occurred during sexual intercourse and physical activities such as jogging and swimming. Physical examination revealed no spontaneous, gaze-evoked, or positional nystagmus. However, left-beating nystagmus was observed following horizontal head-shaking and during vibratory stimuli applied to either mastoid or brow.

A 10-year-old Chinese girl was admitted to our hospital for severe pain along with shortening and deformity of the right leg. Five years prior, at the age of 5, the patient visited our hospital due to limping and mild pain in her right thigh, which intensified with stretching or touch.

A 20-month-old male patient was admitted to the pediatric neurology department with a notably large head. Historical information indicated that his head size had been larger than average since birth. He is the first child of parents who are first-degree cousins. Physical examination revealed significant developmental delay. His weight was recorded at 9kg (below the 3rd percentile), height at 75cm (below the 3rd percentile), and head circumference at 55cm (above the 97th percentile). The patient exhibited a dysmorphic facial appearance, including a flattened nasal root. Bilateral simian lines were also noted during the physical examination.

A 13-year-old female, the youngest of her siblings, presented with a complaint of painless, progressive, and bilateral enlargement of the lower face and jaws. There was no family history of similar conditions. The patient was born full-term with no abnormalities until about the age of 2 years, when bilateral symmetrical prominence of the lower face was observed. This enlargement ceased at around two and a half years of age and remained unchanged for several years. Over the past 3-4 months, her parents noted a gradual increase in size to its current state. Physical examination showed the patient to be well-built, active, and mentally alert. No abnormalities were detected in the chest, abdomen, cardiovascular, or central nervous systems. There were no signs of cutaneous pigmentation, congenital abnormalities, or endocrine disturbances. Extraoral examination revealed normal facial expression and color with no ophthalmic abnormalities. There was diffuse enlargement on both sides of the face extending to the inferior border and angle of the mandible bilaterally, roughly round in shape, hard in consistency, and with ill-defined margins. The swelling was fixed with no secondary changes, and the right side was slightly larger than the left. Palpation revealed normal skin temperature and no tenderness. A single, firm, non-tender, and mobile submandibular lymph node approximately 1 cm in diameter was palpable on the right side. Intraoral examination showed the patient in the permanent dentition stage with the absence of the mandibular left second permanent molar. There was no disturbance in occlusion or shift in the midline.

A 27-year-old male visited the outpatient department exhibiting reduced sweating and minimal body hair. His medical history included asthma with frequent episodes, managed with regular use of inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators. During childhood, he experienced easy overheating due to reduced sweating. His teeth were malformed and cone-shaped, but he received dental replacements 10 years prior. Physical examination revealed frontal bossing, a prominent supraorbital ridge, sunken cheeks, thick lips, sparse hair, scanty eyebrows, and low-set, overfolding ears.

A 21-year-old male from Iran presented with a white, itchy spot on the buccal mucosa. The primary concern was a white bilateral lesion in the oral mucosa, which the patient reported had been present since birth. The patient was in good general health and reported no similar conditions in immediate family members or elsewhere on his body. Clinical examination revealed bilateral, symmetrical white plaques and patches on the buccal and labial mucosa that could not be removed. These plaques were smooth with a velvety texture and had irregular, well-defined borders. There was no elevation or erythema, and the margins were clear with no noticeable lymph nodes. The patient's oral hygiene was good, and other oral structures appeared normal.
